identity.title: Work of breathing: accessory muscle use, tripoding, pursed-lip breathing, inability to speak full sentences

technique.how: Observe from the doorway before touching the patient: sternocleidomastoid/scalene contraction on inspiration, suprasternal or intercostal retraction, tripod posture, pursed-lip exhalation, and diaphoresis. Ask an open question and note whether the patient can finish a sentence in one breath (sentences vs phrases vs single words).
technique.prerequisites: Patient undressed enough to see the neck and chest wall; observe at rest before any intervention if safe to do so.
technique.contraindications: None; it is observation only. Do not delay oxygen, bronchodilator or airway management to complete the assessment.

interpretation.positive_finding: Visible accessory muscle use, tripoding or speech limited to words/phrases marks a severe exacerbation of airflow obstruction (asthma/COPD) or another cause of high work of breathing, and in admitted asthmatics is associated with a markedly lower %FEV1. Treat it as a severity marker, not as a discriminator between causes.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of accessory muscle use does not exclude significant airflow limitation or hypercapnia; a tiring or obtunded patient may lose the sign as ventilatory failure develops.
interpretation.pitfalls: Loss of accessory muscle use with rising drowsiness signals fatigue, not improvement. Obesity, a thick neck and supine positioning hide sternocleidomastoid contraction.
interpretation.changes_what: Present: escalate now (continuous monitoring, blood gas, bronchodilator/NIV or airway plan). Absent: do not use to downgrade severity; rely on oximetry, gas and peak flow.

sources.citation: Holleman DR, Simel DL. Does the clinical examination predict airflow limitation? JAMA. 1995.
Arnold DH, Gebretsadik T, Minton PA, Higgins S, Hartert TV. Clinical measures associated with FEV1 in persons with asthma requiring hospital admission. Am J Emerg Med. 2007.
Atta JA, Nunes MP, Fonseca-Guedes CH, Avena LA, Borgiani MT, Fiorenza RF, Martins MA. Patient and physician evaluation of the severity of acute asthma exacerbations. Braz J Med Biol Res. 2005.
Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA). Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2024 update: assessment of exacerbation severity (talks in words, accessory muscles, drowsiness).

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of the sign to withhold escalation in a drowsy, exhausted or silent-chest patient.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Accessory muscle use plus inability to speak, drowsiness, silent chest, bradycardia or SpO2 <90% = life-threatening exacerbation: immediate senior/ICU involvement.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No sign-level kappa located for adults in the sources reviewed; Holleman 1995 RCE reportedly tabulates sternomastoid contraction reliability but the table was not accessible (unverified recall).

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy estimate (sens/spec/LR) was retrievable. Holleman & Simel 1995 RCE (PMID 7815660) has no PubMed abstract and no PMC text, so its sternomastoid-contraction row could not be quoted. Primary studies found report association with severity only: Arnold 2007 (PMID 17499661) in 129 admitted adult asthmatics: "%FEV1 was significantly lower in participants with accessory muscle use (Median %FEV1 = 37.5%, IQR: 27.0-49.0) than in those without accessory muscle use (Median %FEV1= 55.0%, IQR: 39.0-69.0), (P = .004)" (Abstract, Results); Atta 2005 (PMID 15334197): "Use of neck accessory muscles, expiratory time and wheezing intensity were the explanatory variables in the FEV1 regression model" (Abstract). Neither reports a 2x2, so no estimate entered. Arnold 2011 (PMID 21457886, PMC3074618) is paediatric and also reports only median %FEV1 by muscle-group count. Searches: 'accessory muscle use airflow obstruction physical examination likelihood ratio' (0 hits), 'accessory muscle use hypercapnia dyspnea emergency predictor' (0 hits), Holleman 1993 (PMID 8441077) and Straus 2000 CARE-COAD1 (PMID 10770147) abstracts do not mention accessory muscle use. GINA is cited for the severity-grading use of the sign (guideline, no PMID).
